plan.title: Grade 3 Memory Work & Recitation — Course Plan

sections.title: 1. Purpose and place in the outline

blocks.text: Repetitio mater studiorum est: repetition is the mother of learning (§1). Memory work is the spine of the grammar stage: daily recitation of Scripture, poetry, math facts, Latin forms, timeline events, states and capitals, presidents, science words and hymns (§1, §3G).

The outline is clear that Memory Work is a daily 10–15 minute block, not a standalone subject (§3G). It has almost no content of its own. Every other course sends it something to keep, and its job is to make sure nothing learned this year is forgotten. Its assessment is recitation at the end of each term, before the family or co-op (§3G).

sections.title: 2. One rule: who teaches, who keeps

blocks.text: Several courses already have their own daily drill (Arithmetic's facts, Latin's chants and words, Spelling's rules). To avoid doing the same work twice:
The owning course teaches and drills a thing while it's new. Arithmetic drills ×7 in the week it's learned; Latin drills amō in Term 1.
Memory Work keeps it afterward. Once the owning course moves on, the item comes into Memory Work's review so it isn't lost.
Recitation pieces are Memory Work's own daily work from the start: the term's poem, Scripture passage, catechism, hymn and Latin saying. They're too long to learn in another course's few minutes.
So Memory Work never re-teaches math facts or Latin vocabulary. It keeps the skip-counting chants, the Latin chants and the spelling rules alive once those courses have moved on.
36 weeks in 6 six-week terms.
5 lessons a week, so 30 per term, each 10–15 minutes, in the daily core.
Week 6 of each term ends with Recitation Day.

The year runs on one memory box: an index-card box with tabbed dividers. Each item to be remembered is on its own card. Cards move back through the tabs as they're learned, so review gets less frequent as memory gets stronger. That's spaced repetition, done by hand.

Platform note: this is the daily spaced-repetition queue the outline names as "the most defensible piece of technology in the product" (§9). The paper box and an app version work the same way.

Cards (kept after the owning course moves on)

The term's Scripture passage; the Nicene Creed (T1–2), the Ten Commandments (T3–4), the Lord's Prayer (T5–6); the term's hymn

blocks.text: The two remaining courses, Fine Arts (12) and Physical Education (13), will add their own items (composers, artists, perhaps a few rules of games) once planned.
Many courses end their term with a recitation. Rather than hold five separate ones, Memory Work gathers them into one Recitation Day in week 6 of each term, before the family or co-op:
1. The term's poem (Literature)
2. The term's Scripture passage and catechism (Bible)
3. The Latin saying, and one Latin chant (Latin)
4. A fact recitation: the term's states and capitals, or the timeline dates, as a chant (History and the memory box)
5. The term's hymn, sung (Bible)

It takes about 15 minutes. Keep it warm and celebratory: a small audience, a little ceremony, perhaps a treat afterward. Year-end Recitation Day in week 36 adds the best pieces from the whole year, and coordinates with Literature's year-end recitation and Bible's year-end recitation so they happen together.
Recitation is the assessment (§3G). On Recitation Day the parent notes, for each piece, perfect, nearly, or still learning. It isn't graded.
The memory box shows progress by itself: cards moving toward Archive are known.
Year-end record: which recitation pieces are perfect, and how many cards reached Archive. It's handed to Grade 4, whose memory box begins with this year's Archive.
Memory Work is daily, but a missed day costs little. Pick up at today's Day tab; don't try to catch up missed tabs.
A missed week: spend the first two days of the next week on Daily and Odd/Even only, then resume the full routine.
Too many cards? If the routine runs past 15 minutes, cut the Archive count first, never the recitation pieces.
An index-card box (recipe-box size) with tabbed dividers: Daily, Odd, Even, Day 1 to Day 5, Archive.
Index cards. The child writes many of the cards themselves, which is good handwriting practice and helps fix them in memory.
Printed copies of each term's recitation pieces, kept at the front of the box.

blocks.text: Cards in Archive at year's end: ___
For Grade 4: the year's Archive cards become the start of Grade 4's memory box. Pieces marked "nearly" or "still learning" begin Grade 4 in the Daily tab.

The year's celebration. It brings together the year-end recitations of Literature (week 36), Bible (week 36) and Latin (week 36) into one program. Invite grandparents, friends or the co-op. It runs 25–30 minutes, so hold it in two parts with a break (or across two days) if that suits the child better.
Part 1 — The year's poems and Scripture
1. "The Landing of the Pilgrim Fathers", stanzas 1–5
2. "The Village Blacksmith", stanzas 1–4
3. "Paul Revere's Ride", stanzas 1–3
4. The Preamble, and "We hold these truths…"
5. The Lindsay selection
6. 1 Corinthians 13:4–8a
Literature allows the child to drop one poem if the program is too long; do the same here.
Part 2 — Faith, Latin and facts
7. The Nicene Creed
8. The Ten Commandments
9. The Lord's Prayer
10. The Glōria Patrī, and Repetītiō māter studiōrum est
11. The fifty states and capitals, as a chant
12. The twelve presidents, in order
13. "Amazing Grace", sung

Keep the box going lightly: the recitation pieces once a week, and five Archive cards a day, three days a week. A child who keeps the box alive through the summer starts Grade 4 with the whole year still in hand.

This is the year's crowning moment. A third-grader reciting five poems, six Scripture passages, the Creed, the Commandments, a Latin prayer and all fifty states has done something remarkable. Let the occasion say so.
Calm, not pressure. By week 36 the child has said every piece dozens of times. Treat the day as a performance for people who love them, not a test.
Split it if needed. Two shorter parts are better than one long one for most eight- and nine-year-olds.
